concept.name: Order-flow imbalance
concept.definition: The net excess of demand over supply at the best bid and ask, defined by Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014) from all order book events - limit orders, market orders, and cancellations - at the best prices. They show short-horizon price changes are largely driven by this imbalance, with an approximately linear relation whose slope is inversely proportional to market depth.
concept.intuition: Prices move on the net pressure of orders arriving and leaving the inside market, not on raw trade counts.
concept.mechanics: Each order book event contributes positively when it adds bid-side or removes ask-side quantity and negatively otherwise; the cumulative imbalance over an interval is then related to the contemporaneous mid-price change. Unlike signed trade volume, OFI incorporates quote updates and cancellations.
concept.formula: OFI = sum over events e_n, with e_n = +Dq_b for bid-side quantity increases, -Dq_b for bid-side decreases, and symmetric negative contributions for ask-side events (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov convention).
concept.failure_modes: The linear relation is a short-horizon statistical regularity that breaks down around news jumps and requires full order-event data; estimates degrade when depth is manipulated or rapidly cancelled.
concept.misconceptions: Order-flow imbalance is not just signed trade volume: limit-order submissions and cancellations at the inside move it as much as executed trades do.
concept.example: Over one second, 3,000 net shares are added at the best bid while the ask queue thins; the mid-price typically ticks up by an amount inversely proportional to book depth.

citations.source: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 'The Price Impact of Order Book Events', Journal of Financial Econometrics 12(1):47-88 (arXiv preprint)
